text:
# Line Illustration Detection

Also called: Analytical and pixel-based line detection, Line detection in NPR

## Overview
Line Illustration Detection is a family of Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) techniques designed to detect and render lines that communicate the shape, structure, and boundaries of volumetric data or isosurfaces, solving the problem of visualizing complex geometry like medical models where standard photorealistic rendering may obscure structural details [S1, unofficial]. What sets this family apart from its siblings, such as [Face-based volume rendering with edge highlights](2453-face-based-volume-rendering-with-edge-highlights.md), [Outline and Contour Generation](4137-outline-and-contour-generation.md), and [LOG-based Silhouette Detection](6322-log-based-silhouette-detection.md), is its exclusive focus on generating line-based abstractions rather than silhouette outlines or edge highlights [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The family is unified by the goal of generating line textures or strokes that represent surface shape or boundaries [S1, unofficial]. The core distinction lies in the domain of detection: analytical approaches are vector-oriented and resolution-independent, requiring explicit analytical representations to transform without artifacts [S1, unofficial]; pixel-based approaches operate in image space, often using G-buffers containing geometric properties like colour and depth to detect lines, and are faster and simpler to implement when explicit analytical representations are unavailable [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### Principal Direction Line Texture
A technique for visualizing volume isosurfaces by advecting particles along principal curvature directions to create line textures that communicate surface shape [S1, unofficial]. It is chosen when viewpoint-independent shape communication is required and the volume data allows for the calculation of curvature fields [S1, unofficial]. The method calculates the set of principal directions and principal curvatures in the volume, places an evenly distributed set of tiny opaque particles on the isosurfaces of interest, advects the particles through the vector field defined by the principal directions, and treats the resulting paths as a 3D line texture [S1, unofficial]. Algorithmic efficiency and artistic line quality must be addressed for NPR applicability, as showing line direction alone is not necessarily sufficient for an aesthetically pleasing rendering [S1, unofficial].

### Copper Plate Etching Simulation
A technique simulating copper plate etching by intersecting a scene with closely-spaced, equidistant, parallel planes to detect surface curves [S1, unofficial]. It is chosen when a traditional artistic style is desired or when surface curves need to be highlighted via intersection logic [S1, unofficial]. The method intersects the scene with a set of closely-spaced, equidistant, parallel planes, uses a modified ray tracer to detect the surface curves resulting from these intersections, and uses G-buffers containing geometric properties such as colour and depth to modulate the final line style [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of line illustration in volume visualization draws from historical printing techniques [S1, unofficial]. Copper plate printing was used for centuries in scientific publications because it existed before modern photographic reproduction [S1, unofficial]. Leister simulated this by intersecting scenes with parallel planes [S1, unofficial]. In the context of digital volume visualization, Interrante introduced a novel line illustration technique in 1997 [S1, unofficial]. This work was motivated by perceptual psychology literature suggesting that lines in the principal directions of curvature communicate surface shape better than lines in other directions [S1, unofficial]. The technique was developed to address the complexity of medical models, which share traits with other complex geometries [S1, unofficial]. Analytical approaches are noted for their flexibility and resolution independence [S1, unofficial]. Pixel-based methods, such as those using G-buffers introduced by Saito and Takahashi, offer an alternative when analytical models are not available [S1, unofficial]. Hertzmann surveyed image space outline generation algorithms in 1999, noting that simple outlines can be generated by extracting edges from depth maps [S1, unofficial].
